newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Nordic aid agencies protest to Afghan Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Nordic aid agencies protest to Afghan Taleban.

text.p: A group of aid agencies based in the Nordic countries has issued a statement expressing concern over policies of the purist Islamic Taleban movement and threatened to review their presence in Taleban-controlled parts of Afghanistan.

"We, the Nordic non-governmental organisations (NGOs) active in Afghanistan, want to express our concern about recent regulations issued by the Taleban authorities, which contradict the humanitarian principles on which our work is founded," said the statement, which was issued in Pakistan on Monday. A copy of the statement was obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.
"We are also concerned about actions taken by different Taleban authorities which have affected our operations in Afghanistan," it said.
The statement was signed by four agencies: the Danish Committee for Aid to Afghan Refugees, Norwegian Afghanistan Committee, Norwegian Church Aid and the Swedish Committee for Afghanistan.
It was issued before Jan Eglund, the Norwegian Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, is due to visit Kabul on Wednesday to meet Taleban officials and view aid programmes.
Eglund will be the most senior western official to visit Kabul since the Taleban took the city last September. Norway is one of the largest contributors of aid to Afghanistan.
"The regulations we are referring to are: that NGOs are prohibited to work in areas not under the control of the Taleban," the statement said.
"For instance, the governor of Ghazni province (south of Kabul) has explicitly forbidden NGOs with offices in Ghazni town to work in districts in one of the province which are part of the Hazarajat."
Most of the mountainous Hazarajat region, which borders Ghazni, is under the control of groups opposed to the Taleban.

The statement said if the agencies were stopped from providing aid in accordance with the principle of supporting those in need regardless of gender, political, religious and ethnic affiliation, they would reconsider their programmes in Taleban-controlled areas of Afghanistan.

"If we were prevented or obstructed to implement our activities in accordance with those principles, we will be forced to consider the possibility of reviewing our involvement in Taleban-controlled areas of Afghanistan," it said.
The statement also said that a series of decrees issued on July 16 by the Taleban's religious police has obstructed their ability to reach some of Afghanistan's more vulnerable groups.
The decrees limit aid agencies' access to women, and their ability to employ them.
"The ability of NGOs to provide support to vulnerable groups, in particular women, has been obstructed by the July 16 regulations," the statement said.

Care International, one of the world's largest aid agencies, has suspended operations in Kabul in the wake of the new regulations. Care said they would be forced to break their basic principles if they followed the regulations.

The statement also highlighted a number of recent mass arrests in which many NGO workers were caught. It said the arrests contravened internationally recognised principles of justice and protocols signed by the Taleban authorities and the NGOs.
It called on Taleban authorities to guarantee the security of NGO staff.
"If this request cannot be complied with, we will find it increasingly difficult to implement our programmes in areas where such actions are permitted by the Taleban authorities," the statement said.
